strengths: The problem is well motivated. Figure 1 gives a clear analytical example where choosing interventions using context achieves expected reward 1/3, while the specified CoBO scope achieves zero.
Combining graph-based POMPS pruning with contextual Bayesian optimization provides a simple, modular approach to causal policy optimization with continuous variables.

Experiments cover settings where baselines can and cannot attain the optimum, report 110 seeds with uncertainty intervals, and demonstrate benefits from removing redundant variables. The paper also acknowledges cases where CoBO converges faster.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The algorithm combines existing POMPS theory, HEBO, and standard UCB selection. The extension to continuous domains is useful, but the paper provides little new analysis or sufficiently broad empirical evidence to establish a substantial advance over the cited mixed-policy optimization literature.

The scope-selection justification is incomplete. Each arm's reward distribution changes as its HEBO policy learns, so standard stationary-bandit UCB guarantees do not directly apply. Observing that rewards become stationary at optimality does not establish that the coupled algorithm reaches optimality. Decreasing normalized regret over 700 iterations also does not establish asymptotic sublinear regret or the conclusion's claim of always achieving the optimum.

The general policy class is not adequately connected to the implementation. Definition 3.1 permits action-specific contexts and contexts generated after earlier interventions, whereas Section 4 uses a joint acquisition maximization with the context vector given. The paper does not explain how this implements sequential policies without using information unavailable when an action must be chosen.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed UCB selector's contribution. There are no comparisons against uniform allocation or acquisition-based selection using identical POMPS sets and BO models. Both PSA configurations contain only one POMPS for CoCa-BO, so those comparisons cannot demonstrate benefits from its bandit selector. Comparisons against structurally restricted baselines primarily establish the value of the richer policy class.

Evaluation is narrow: two small graph families and an extension constructed with many redundant variables. Every experiment has at most two candidate POMPSes. There are no tests with many competing scopes, enumeration-cost measurements, or runtime scaling results, leaving the claimed efficiency in large systems insufficiently supported.

Several mathematical inconsistencies affect reproducibility and interpretation. Appendix A.2 omits Cancer from the PSA structural equation but subsequently substitutes it to derive a different objective and optimum. Appendix C specifies C4 as normally distributed around itself, inconsistent with the acyclic model. Section 5 defines regret as observed reward minus optimal expected reward, which has the wrong sign for the maximization experiments. These require correction and confirmation of which equations generated the results.

Implementation details are insufficient: UCB exploration settings, initialization, GP configurations, several intervention domains, and baseline configurations are not clearly specified. The manuscript states that code is shared but provides no repository link.
